edits.heading: Example
edits.before:
Assume Countable Choice.

Let the real periodic Fourier coefficient space be $X=Y=\mathbb R\oplus\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R^2)$, with one constant coordinate and cosine–sine coordinate pairs for each positive frequency, and give it the canonical inner product $\langle(c_0,(a_n,b_n)),(d_0,(c_n,d_n))\rangle=c_0d_0+\sum_{n\ge1}(a_nc_n+b_nd_n)$. The interleaving map $(c_0,(a_n,b_n))\mapsto(c_0,a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots)$ is an isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so this is a real Hilbert space. For a heat time $\bar t>0$, define the periodic heat forward operator by
$$
T_{\bar t}(c_0,(a_n,b_n)_{n\ge1})=(c_0,(e^{-n^2\bar t}a_n,e^{-n^2\bar t}b_n)_{n\ge1}).
$$
Its eigenvalues for $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$ are $1$ on the constant mode and $e^{-2n^2\bar t}$ on both modes of frequency $n$. The singular system for the sequence model is ordered as the constant mode, then cosine and sine modes in increasing positive frequency; its singular values are nonincreasing. Use the truth whose function is $f^\dagger(x)=\pi/2-|x|$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$, and observe its weak Gaussian white-noise data with known standard deviation $\sigma>0$. Li and Werner report an empirical SOLIT simulation at $\bar t=0.1$ using $10^4$ Monte Carlo runs: SOLIT appears close to the oracle, while the minimax behavior is unclear and the empirical adaptation behavior for spectral cut-off is irregular. These are reported simulation findings, not a theorem or a simulation performed for this library.

For the spectral-cutoff candidate sequence $\alpha_n=e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0$, the variance sums $V_n=1+2\sum_{k=1}^n e^{2k^2\bar t}$ do not have a uniformly bounded consecutive ratio: $V_n/V_{n-1}\to\infty$. Thus this infinite spectral-cutoff sequence does not meet the uniform geometric-variance-grid condition. A continuous Tikhonov filter $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ does admit such a grid because its variance function is continuous, decreases from $+\infty$ to $0$, and can be sampled at successive fixed variance ratios.

edits.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $B,C>0$ and $0<b<1$. Let $g\in C^1(\mathbb C;\mathbb C)$, let $\ell\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and suppose $g(0)=0$ and
$$|g(k)-\ell k|\le C|k|^{1-b}\qquad(|k|\ge1).$$
Suppose distributionally $\bar\partial g=\sigma g+E$, where $\sigma$ is measurable, $\|\sigma\|_\infty\le B$, $E\in C^1$, and for $0<\delta\le1/2$,
$$|E(k)|\le C\delta e^{C|k|},\qquad |\nabla E(k)|\le C e^{C(1+|k|)}.$$
There exist $D>0$ and $\delta_0\in(0,1/2)$, depending only on $B,C,b$, such that
$$|\ell|\ge D[\log(1/\delta)]^{-b},\quad0<\delta<\delta_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(k)\ne0\text{ for every }k\ne0.$$
If $E=0$, the same conclusion holds for every $\ell\ne0$, without a threshold condition.

edits.before: Define a procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ on a finite planar code $D$ for one oriented knot and a designated under-arc $a_0$ as follows. First check all incidence, valence, branch-pairing, crossing over/under, edge-orientation, and one-component conditions in the code. For each pair of rational line segments in the drawing certificate, compute the determinant of their direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate linear intersection equations and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Accept an intersection only when it is a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence, and at a crossing verify that the two branch direction vectors have nonzero determinant. Reject self-intersections and all unrecorded intersections. If any check fails, return `invalid-input`. Otherwise traverse the oriented knot once starting at $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. For each crossing $v$, read its oriented over-tangent and positive in-plane normal. Let $a_s$ be the under-side from which that normal points and $a_t$ the side toward which it points, and read the over-arc $a_o$. Append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. Equivalently, if the incoming under-tangent follows that normal, append $x_o^{-1}x_{\rm in}x_ox_{\rm out}^{-1}$; otherwise append $x_ox_{\rm in}x_o^{-1}x_{\rm out}^{-1}$. The orientation of a positive meridian is fixed locally by requiring the knot tangent followed by the normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and this one relator per crossing.
edits.after:
The input is a finite record $D$ and a designated starting under-arc $a_0$ of one oriented knot. First check that the vertex, edge, and segment lists are finite; that every vertex, bend, and point on an edge polyline has rational coordinates; and that each polyline has the prescribed incident endpoints. Before geometric tests, delete consecutive repeated coordinates from each polyline; reject an edge with no positive-length segment or a crossing with a zero-length incident ray. Check that every crossing has four incident half-edges, a recorded cyclic order and a pairing into alternating opposite branches, and one designated over-branch; every other vertex must be a valence-two bend. Check that edge orientations agree at bends and continue coherently through each paired branch, and that following these pairings and bends traces one oriented circle. If $a_0$ is not one of the resulting under-arcs, or any structural check fails, return invalid-input.

For every unordered pair of line segments, compute the determinant of their rational direction vectors. If it is nonzero, solve the two-coordinate intersection equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ and check whether the solution lies on both closed segments. If the determinant is zero, test collinearity and overlap by exact rational determinant and endpoint-order comparisons. Reject every self-intersection, every positive-length overlap, and every intersection except a shared declared bend or crossing vertex with the recorded incidence. At each crossing, sort the four nonzero incident rays by half-plane and exact determinant comparisons; reject the input if two rays have the same direction, if this geometric cyclic order disagrees with the recorded order, or if the paired branches do not alternate. These checks are finite.

After validation, traverse the oriented knot once from $a_0$, label the maximal under-arcs $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, and introduce one symbol $x_i$ for the positive meridian of each $a_i$. At each crossing, let the outgoing over-half-edge be the ray in the direction of the oriented over-tangent. In the verified counterclockwise cyclic order, the under-half-edge immediately following it is the target side $a_t$; the other under-half-edge is the source side $a_s$. Read the over-arc $a_o$ and append exactly the relator $x_o^{-1}x_sx_ox_t^{-1}$. This rule uses the positive in-plane normal, which points counterclockwise from the oriented over-tangent, and does not depend on the under-strand direction. The orientation of each positive meridian is fixed by requiring the oriented knot tangent followed by its normal-disk orientation to give the ambient orientation. Once a complement basepoint and basing paths to the meridians are fixed, interpret $x_i$ as the corresponding based positive meridian. Return the finite group presentation with generators $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ and one relator per crossing.

Input an integer $m\ge1$, a table $T\in\{1,\ldots,m\}^{m\times m}$ with
entry $T[x,y]$ intended to be $x*y$, a mode "rack" or "quandle", a finite
regular oriented link diagram $D$ with $a$ arcs and $c$ crossings, and fixed
finite orderings of its arcs and crossings. If the table is not $m\times m$,
return invalid-table-shape with its row lengths. If an entry is outside
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$, return invalid-table-entry with its row, column, and value.
Otherwise perform these checks in order:

1. For each $y=1,\ldots,m$, check whether the column
   $(T[1,y],\ldots,T[m,y])$ is a permutation of $\{1,\ldots,m\}$. If not,
   return right-translation-not-bijective with $y$, a repeated value and a
   missing value.
2. For each ordered triple $(x,y,z)$ in lexicographic order, check
   $T[T[x,y],z]=T[T[x,z],T[y,z]]$. If not, return
   self-distributivity-fails with $(x,y,z)$ and both table values.
3. In quandle mode, check $T[x,x]=x$ for each $x$ in increasing order. If
   not, return idempotency-fails with $x$ and $T[x,x]$.

If the selected axioms pass, enumerate the $m^a$ functions from the supplied
ordered arcs of $D$ to $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in lexicographic order. Retain an assignment
exactly when it satisfies the crossing rule in the rack/quandle Definition,
using the inverse column permutation when the rule calls for the right
division. Return the retained assignments and their number. No correctness or
complexity claim is part of this algorithm's Definition.

edits.heading: Definition
edits.before:
A **rack** is a set $R$ with a binary operation $*:R\times R\to R$ such
that for every $y\in R$ the right translation $R_y(x)=x*y$ is a bijection
and $(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$ for all $x,y,z\in R$. A **quandle** is a rack
satisfying $x*x=x$ for every $x$. For either structure, write
$x\mathbin{\bar *}y=R_y^{-1}(x)$.

For a regular oriented link diagram $D$, let $A(D)$ be its finite set of
maximal under-arcs. Form the set of finite terms recursively: each symbol
$x_a$ for $a\in A(D)$ is a term, and if $s,t$ are terms then $s*t$ and
$s\mathbin{\bar *}t$ are terms. Let $\sim$ be the intersection of all
equivalence relations on these terms that are compatible with both operations
and contain the quandle identities: idempotency, right invertibility, and
right self-distributivity, together with the crossing relations.
At a crossing with source and target under-arcs $u,v$ and overarc $o$, the
crossing relation is $x_v=x_u*x_o$; reversing source and target gives the
equivalent relation with $\bar *$. The quotient term set $Q(D)$ is the
**diagram quandle**, or the diagram presentation of the **fundamental
quandle**. Its independence of diagram is proved in the Theorem.

For any quandle $Q$, its **adjoint group** $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ is the
group presentation with generators $e_q$ for all $q\in Q$ and relators
$e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$ for all $q,r\in Q$. A group presentation
$\langle X\mid S\rangle$ means the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the
normal closure of the relator words $S$.

The diagram presentation and the adjoint group are algebraic constructions;
this definition makes no completeness or knot-classification assertion.

edits.before: Assume full AC. Let $M=E_{P(K)}$ be a satellite knot exterior with companion torus $T_c$. Suppose the pattern hypotheses of the essential-companion-torus lemma hold, both components of $M$ cut along $T_c$ are atoroidal or Seifert-fibered, and $M$ itself is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Then the inclusion-minimal JSJ system of $M$ consists of a torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. **Input and output.** The input is one finite ASCII string. Its prescribed form is

no whitespace or trailing character. The output is either the rejection symbol
`REJECT` or an element of the coefficient extension $T$ with $a=\rho$ and
$d=\delta$.

   $\ell$ is not the number of letter tokens, if $n=0$, or if any token index
   fails $1\le i<n$, return `REJECT` and halt. Otherwise read the tokens as the
   finite signed Artin word
   $$\beta=\sigma_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_\ell}^{\varepsilon_\ell}, \qquad \varepsilon_j\in\{-1,1\}.$$

2. **Compute the closure data.** Form the BMW product
   $b_\beta=g_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots g_{i_\ell}^{\varepsilon_\ell}$.
   Set $w=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\varepsilon_j$ and let $c$ be the number of cycles,
   including fixed points, of the permutation $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ of
   $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

3. **Enumerate a matching basis.** Work in the unit rectangle with top and
   bottom endpoints at $(j/(n+1),1)$ and $(j/(n+1),0)$, respectively, for
   $1\le j\le n$. Fix a prefix-free binary encoding of finite rational
   polygonal diagrams with over/under data, with rational coordinates written
   as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs. Number the tangle endpoints in cyclic order
   $1,2,\ldots,n,\bar n,\ldots,\bar2,\bar1$. Enumerate perfect matchings
   recursively: pair the least unmatched endpoint with each greater unmatched
   endpoint in increasing order, then continue on the remaining endpoints. For
   each matching $\mu$, scan finite diagram codes in increasing code length and
   then lexicographically. Choose the first code of a rational polygonal tangle
   diagram with that connector, no closed component and no strand self-crossing,
   in which the open strands are oriented from their lower-numbered to their
   higher-numbered endpoint, ordered by initial endpoint, and every crossing is
   over on the first traversed strand. This is the standard descending
   representative $T_\mu$. Give each polygonal segment its distinct code label
   and its orientation inherited from its strand. The standard descending
   matching spanning lemma guarantees that such codes exist and that they all
   represent the same tangle class for each $\mu$.

4. **Build generator matrices by skein reduction.** For every signed generator
   $g_i^{\pm1}$, form its left-multiplication matrix in the ordered basis
   $\{T_\mu\}$. The column at $T_\mu$ is computed by reducing
   $g_i^{\pm1}T_\mu$. In each current diagram, orient open strands from the
   smaller to the larger endpoint label and order them by their initial
   endpoints. Order each closed component by the least label of its polygonal
   segments, start at the initial end of that segment, and follow its stored
   orientation. Traverse the strands in that order and select the first
   crossing whose first encountered branch is under. Segment labels are
   retained through crossing switches and smoothings. Let $R(D)$ denote the
   coordinate vector of the current tangle expression in the matching basis.
   If the selected crossing is $D_+$ in the fixed chart, put $\eta=1$; if it
   is $D_-$, put $\eta=-1$. Replace
   $$R(D)=R(D^{\mathrm{sw}})+\eta z_D\bigl(R(D_0)-R(D_\infty)\bigr),$$
   using the fixed through smoothing $D_0$ and cup-cap smoothing $D_\infty$.
   Recurse on all three resulting terms. The switched branch has one fewer
   non-descending crossing and each smoothing has one fewer crossing. At a
   descending tangle leaf, use the traversal to lift each already traversed
   segment over the remaining diagram, removing self-crossings while fixing
   the boundary; retain crossings between distinct open strands in their
   ordered layers. Remove the resulting framing curls with factors $a$ or
   $a^{-1}$ and each closed component with factor $d$. Record the remaining
   standard matching tangle and add its coefficient to that matching coordinate.

5. **Apply the matrices and evaluate the trace row.** Start with the coordinate
   vector of the identity tangle and apply the generator matrices from the
   rightmost braid letter to the leftmost, obtaining $v_\beta$, the coordinate
   vector of $\Phi_n(b_\beta)$. For each matching $\mu$, close $T_\mu$ by the
   first code in the same finite-code order for pairwise disjoint rational
   polygonal arcs outside the rectangle joining corresponding top and bottom
   endpoints without a twist. Orient each such arc from its smaller to larger
   cyclic endpoint label. Evaluate this closed diagram by the same deterministic
   traversal and skein recursion: at a descending leaf, straighten the
   traversal-ordered components, remove their framing curls with factors
   $a,a^{-1}$, remove each free circle with factor $d$, and use
   $P(\varnothing)=1$ for the empty diagram. Set
   $$t_\mu=d^{-n}P(\widehat{T_\mu}),\qquad \tau_n(b_\beta)=t^{\mathsf T}v_\beta.$$

6. **Return**
   $$-(-1)^c a^{-w}d^{n-1}\tau_n(b_\beta).$$
   All matrices and recursion trees are finite, all coefficients lie in $T$,
   and no division by the skein variable is used.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented knot diagram with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ and a marked point $p$ away from crossings. Put $\mathbb A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$ and $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. At a resolution state $v\in\{0,1\}^n$, let $V_v$ be the free abelian group generated by the resolution circles, order its circle generators, and use the exterior algebra $\Lambda^*V_v$ as its state module. A wedge of $r$ distinct circle generators has circle quantum degree $k(v)-2r$, where $k(v)=\operatorname{rank}V_v$; its total normalized degrees are $i(v)=|v|-n_-$ and $q=|v|+n_+-2n_-+k(v)-2r$. For a merge saddle joining circles $C_1,C_2$, let $p:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ be the quotient sending both to the merged circle and fixing the other generators; the edge map is $\Lambda^*p$. For a split saddle replacing $C$ by $C_1,C_2$, let $j:V_v\to V_{v+e}$ send $C$ to $C_1$ and fix the other generators; the unsigned edge map is $z\mapsto(C_1-C_2)\wedge\Lambda^*j(z)$. Choosing $C_2$ instead of $C_1$ gives the same map, while reversing the order of $C_1,C_2$ changes only its sign. Multiply each edge map by a sign $\epsilon(e)\in\{1,-1\}$, incorporating any circle-generator reordering sign. The direct sum of these state modules with the resulting cube differential is the odd Khovanov cochain complex $C_o(D)$. Write $Z_p$ for the circle containing the mark. Use the right action $z\cdot X=z\wedge Z_p$, making $C_o(D)$ a complex of right $\mathbb A$-modules; since $\mathbb A$ is commutative these are also ordinary modules over that ring. The action has quantum degree $-2$.

The square condition is that the sum of the two signed saddle composites around each two-dimensional cube face is zero. An edge sign function satisfying it is called square-compatible; existence and invariance require separate proofs.

Let $\mathbb R=\mathbb Z[h,X]/(X^2-hX)$, with $\deg_q(h)=\deg_q(X)=-2$. Its Frobenius structure has unit $\eta(1)=1$, counit $\epsilon(1)=0,\epsilon(X)=1$, quotient-ring multiplication, and comultiplication
$$ \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1-h\,1\otimes1,\qquad \Delta(X)=X\otimes X. $$
Applying these operations to the same normalized cube gives the Bar–Natan cochain complex $C_h(D)$, with circle labels $1,X$ of quantum degrees $1,-1$ and the same normalized state shifts; it is a complex of free $\mathbb R$-modules, and the marked circle acts by multiplication by $X$.

Put $\mathbb B=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)=\mathbb R/(2,h)$. Modulo $2$, the odd exterior basis vector $C_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge C_{i_r}$ corresponds to the even tensor state labeling the selected circles $C_{i_j}$ by $X$ and all other circles by $1$. This statewise bijection defines the candidate comparison $f_D:C_o(D)\otimes\mathbb F_2\to C_h(D)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B$ after setting $h=0$.

A **local even–odd (LEO) triple** is a triple $(C,D,f)$ consisting of a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $C$ free over $\mathbb A$, a finitely generated bigraded cochain complex $D$ free over $\mathbb R$, and a bigraded $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy equivalence
$$ f:C\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb F_2\longrightarrow D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb B, \qquad \mathbb B=\mathbb R/(2,h)=\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2), $$
such that $D[h^{-1}]$ is chain homotopy equivalent over $\mathbb R[h^{-1}]$ to one free rank-one module supported in cohomological degree $0$ and odd quantum degree. For a based knot diagram the intended candidate is $(C_o(D),C_h(D),f_D)$, where $f_D$ identifies the reduced edge maps modulo $2$ and $h$; its satisfaction of the homotopy and localization conditions is a separate theorem.

A local map $(C,D,f)\to(C',D',f')$ is a pair of bigraded module chain maps $\alpha:C\to C'$ and $\beta:D\to D'$ such that $\beta[h^{-1}]$ is a chain homotopy equivalence and the square induced by $f,f',\alpha,\beta$ after quotienting by $(2,h)$ commutes up to an $\mathbb F_2[X]/(X^2)$-linear chain homotopy. Two LEO triples are locally equivalent when there is a local map in each direction.
